question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Bite off more than you can chew
(Constable GD Examination 2022)
options: Too courageous
Overcome gluttony
Take on a task that you cannot finish
Destructive power
solution:
The correct answer is: Take on a task that you cannot finish

Explanation:
"Bite off more than you can chew" - "जितना संभाल सकें, उससे अधिक की जिम्मेदारी लेना"
This idiom means to take on more responsibility or work than one can handle, leading to difficulty in completing it. The correct option aligns perfectly with this meaning.

Origin of the Idiom:
The phrase originates from the literal act of taking a bite of food that is too large to chew comfortably. Over time, it evolved into a metaphor for overcommitting oneself in tasks or responsibilities.

Example:
"He agreed to organize three events in one week but soon realized he had bitten off more than he could chew."
"उसने एक हफ्ते में तीन कार्यक्रम आयोजित करने की जिम्मेदारी ली, लेकिन जल्द ही उसे एहसास हुआ कि उसने अपनी क्षमता से अधिक काम ले लिया है।"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "Bite off more than you can chew" is "Take on a task that you cannot finish" because it directly refers to overcommitting beyond one's capacity. The other options do not relate to the idiom's intended meaning.

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.
On account of
(MTS Non Tech Havaldar CBIC and CBN Examination 2022)
options: Because of
To mark one’s territory
To make excuses
To settle dues
solution:
The correct answer is: Because of

Explanation:
"On account of" - "की वजह से"
The phrase "on account of" is used to indicate the reason or cause behind something, which aligns perfectly with the meaning of "because of."

Origin of the Idiom:
The phrase "on account of" originates from financial and legal contexts, where "account" referred to a record or explanation of transactions. Over time, it evolved to signify causation in general language.

Example:
"The match was postponed on account of heavy rain."
"भारी बारिश की वजह से मैच स्थगित कर दिया गया।"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "on account of" is "because of" since it directly conveys the reason for an action or event. The other options are unrelated to the idiom's intended meaning.

question:
Select the sentence that uses the given idiom correctly.Skating on thin ice
(SICPO Paper I 2024)
options: They were on thin ice due to the icy conditions on the road.
They were on thin ice when they skated on the frozen lake.
He was on thin ice after making a controversial statement.
She was on thin ice while trying to balance on a tightrope.
solution:
The correct answer is: He was on thin ice after making a controversial statement.

Explanation:
"Skating on thin ice" - "खतरनाक स्थिति में होना"
The idiom means being in a risky or precarious situation where one wrong move could lead to trouble. In this context, making a controversial statement puts the person in a delicate position where they might face backlash or consequences.

Origin of the Idiom:
The phrase originates from the literal danger of skating on thin ice, which could crack and cause the skater to fall into freezing water. Over time, it evolved into a metaphor for any risky situation.

Example:
"If you keep lying to your boss, you're skating on thin ice."
"अगर तुम अपने बॉस को झूठ बोलते रहोगे, तो तुम खतरनाक स्थिति में हो।"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "He was on thin ice after making a controversial statement." is "being in a risky situation" because the person is in danger of facing negative consequences due to their statement. The other options either misinterpret the idiom literally or use unrelated contexts.

question:
Select the correct idiom that can substitute the italicised group of words in the given sentence.

To succeed in competitive exams is not an easy task.
(Constable GD Examination 2022)
options:
a black sheep

cat’s paw

child’s play

a bed of thorns
solution:
The correct answer is Option 4, i.e., a bed of thorns.

• Concept involved: Idioms and Phrases
Explanation:
The phrase “not an easy task” refers to something very difficult.
The idiom “a bed of thorns” means a situation full of difficulties and hardships.
Why other options are incorrect:

  • a black sheep → a disreputable member of a group 
  • cat’s paw → a person used by others for their own purpose 
  • child’s play → something very easy 

Hence, the correct idiom is 'a bed of thorns.'

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom in the given sentence.

Rina’s house is at a stone’s throw from the school.
(MTS Non Tech Havaldar CBIC and CBN Examination 2023)
options: A very short distance
Next to
A very long distance
Not very close to
solution:
The correct answer is: A very short distance

Explanation:
"At a stone’s throw" - "पत्थर फेंकने की दूरी पर"
This idiom means a very short distance because it refers to how far a stone can be thrown—typically not very far. In the given sentence, it implies that Rina’s house is very close to the school.

Origin of the Idiom:
The phrase likely comes from the idea that a stone can only be thrown a short distance, making it a metaphor for proximity. It has been used in English since at least the 16th century to describe something being nearby.

Example:
"The beach is just a stone’s throw from our hotel."
"समुद्र तट हमारे होटल से बस पत्थर फेंकने की दूरी पर है।"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "a stone’s throw" is "a very short distance" because it accurately describes something being nearby. The other options either suggest the opposite meaning or do not fit the idiom’s context.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Still waters run deep.
(Junior Assistant (Fire Services))
options: One should be aware of the dangers of depth of the ocean.
People who are silent are often intelligent.
It is better to sail when the tide is high.
Fools pretend to be good speakers.
solution:
The correct answer is: People who are silent are often intelligent.

Explanation:
"Still waters run deep" - "शांत जल गहरा होता है"
This idiom suggests that quiet or reserved individuals often possess profound thoughts, intelligence, or hidden depths of character.

Origin of the Idiom:
The phrase originates from the observation that calm water bodies, like ponds or lakes, often have great depth beneath their serene surface. Similarly, people who appear quiet may have deep wisdom or complex personalities.

Example:
"She rarely speaks in meetings, but when she does, her insights are brilliant—still waters run deep."
"वह मीटिंग्स में कम बोलती है, लेकिन जब बोलती है, तो उसके विचार उत्कृष्ट होते हैं—शांत जल गहरा होता है।"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "Still waters run deep" is "People who are silent are often intelligent." because it metaphorically links calmness with hidden depth. The other options misinterpret the idiom's figurative meaning.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.A doubting Thomas
(Stenographer)
options: A hopeless case, a person or situation having no hope of positive change.
A skeptic who needs physical or personal evidence in order to believe something
A foolish person to lose his/ her money
You cannot change who you are
solution:
The correct answer is: A skeptic who needs physical or personal evidence in order to believe something

Explanation:
"A doubting Thomas" - "शक्की व्यक्ति, जो किसी बात पर विश्वास करने के लिए प्रत्यक्ष प्रमाण चाहता है"
This idiom refers to someone who refuses to believe something without concrete proof, much like the biblical figure Thomas, who doubted Jesus' resurrection until he saw and touched His wounds.

Origin of the Idiom:
The phrase originates from the New Testament of the Bible, specifically the Gospel of John (20:24-29). Thomas, one of Jesus' disciples, refused to believe in Jesus' resurrection until he physically saw and touched His wounds. Hence, the term "Doubting Thomas" became synonymous with skepticism.

Example:
"She didn’t believe the news until she saw it herself—she’s such a doubting Thomas."
"वह खबर पर तब तक विश्वास नहीं करती थी जब तक उसने खुद नहीं देख लिया—वह बहुत शक्की है।"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "A doubting Thomas" is "a skeptic who needs physical or personal evidence in order to believe something" because it directly relates to the biblical story of Thomas, who demanded proof before believing. The other options do not align with this idiom's historical and contextual meaning.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Go back to the drawing board
(Selection Post Higher Secondary Level)
options: Work hard to succeed
Go backwards as the road is closed
Start planning all over again
Have a totally different strategy
solution:
The correct answer is: Start planning all over again

Explanation:
"Go back to the drawing board" - "फिर से योजना बनाना शुरू करें"
This idiom means to start over from the beginning because the previous attempt or plan failed. It implies reevaluating and redesigning a strategy.

Origin of the Idiom:
The phrase originates from the literal act of returning to a drawing board (used by architects, engineers, or designers) to revise or rework a design after an initial failure. It became popular in the mid-20th century.

Example:
"Our marketing campaign didn’t bring results, so we have to go back to the drawing board."
"हमारा मार्केटिंग अभियान सफल नहीं रहा, इसलिए हमें फिर से योजना बनानी होगी।"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "Go back to the drawing board" is "Start planning all over again" because it signifies restarting the planning process after a setback. The other options do not align with the idiom's intended meaning.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Play for time
(Constable GD 2021)
options: To make excuses or do things to gain time
To do something in the stipulated time
To play music in the time provided
To play something for the sake of old times
solution:
The correct answer is: To make excuses or do things to gain time

Explanation:
"Play for time" - "समय निकालने के लिए बहाने बनाना या कार्य करना"
This idiom means deliberately delaying or stalling an action to create more time, often by making excuses or engaging in irrelevant activities.

Origin of the Idiom:
The phrase likely originates from strategic delays in games or negotiations, where one side intentionally prolongs the process to gain an advantage or avoid an immediate unfavorable outcome.

Example:
"The politician tried to play for time by giving vague answers during the debate."
"नेता ने बहस के दौरान अस्पष्ट जवाब देकर समय निकालने की कोशिश की।"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "Play for time" is "To make excuses or do things to gain time" because it refers to intentionally delaying actions to extend a situation. The other options do not align with this idiomatic usage.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom.Meera wanted to prove to those around her that she was nota fair-weather friend.
(Stenographer Grade C and D Examination 2024 )
options: Reliable friend in tough times
Unreliable friend in difficult times
Friend for all situations
Helping and caring companion
solution:
The correct answer is: Unreliable friend in difficult times

Explanation:
"Fair-weather friend" - "मुसीबत में साथ छोड़ने वाला दोस्त"
A "fair-weather friend" is someone who is only around during good times but abandons you in difficult situations. The idiom contrasts with a true, loyal friend.

Origin of the Idiom:
The phrase comes from sailing, where "fair weather" means calm and pleasant conditions. A "fair-weather sailor" only sails when conditions are good, similarly, a "fair-weather friend" is only supportive when circumstances are favorable.

Example:
"Rahul turned out to be a fair-weather friend when he stopped talking to me after I lost my job."
"जब मैंने नौकरी खो दी तो राहुल मुझसे बात करना बंद कर दिया, वह मुसीबत में साथ छोड़ने वाला दोस्त निकला।"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "fair-weather friend" is "unreliable in difficult times" because it describes someone who deserts others during hardships. The other options describe loyal or supportive friends, which are opposite to the idiom's meaning.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Out of sight, out of mind.
(Junior Administrative Assistant)
options: If you don't see something for a long time, it will be forgotten.
A risky situation.
Safe from trouble or anger.
Opposite side or view point.
solution:
The correct answer is: If you don't see something for a long time, it will be forgotten.

Explanation:
"Out of sight, out of mind" - "आँख ओझल, दिल से उतर जाना"
This idiom means that people tend to forget or stop thinking about things or people they do not see regularly. The correct option fits because it directly conveys the idea that absence leads to fading memory or neglect.

Origin of the Idiom:
The phrase dates back to the 13th century and was popularized in English by John Heywood's 1546 proverb collection. It reflects the human tendency to prioritize what is immediately visible or present.

Example:
"After moving abroad, she rarely called her old friends—out of sight, out of mind."
"विदेश जाने के बाद, वह अपने पुराने दोस्तों को शायद ही कभी फोन करती थी—आँख ओझल, दिल से उतर जाना।"

Conclusion:

question:
Choose the most appropriate meaning of the idiom given below:
Ignorance is bliss
(Assistant Superintendent)
options: You're better off not knowing
You're just as bad as I am
This isn't over yet
Get two things done with a single action
solution:
The correct answer is: You're better off not knowing

Explanation:
"Ignorance is bliss" - "अज्ञानता ही सुख है"
This idiom suggests that sometimes not knowing certain information can lead to peace of mind or happiness, implying that knowing the truth might cause distress.

Origin of the Idiom:
The phrase originates from Thomas Gray's 1742 poem "Ode on a Distant Prospect of Eton College," where he wrote: "Where ignorance is bliss, 'tis folly to be wise." It reflects the idea that unawareness can sometimes shield a person from worry or sorrow.

Example:
"She decided not to read the negative comments online—ignorance is bliss."
"उसने ऑनलाइन नकारात्मक टिप्पणियाँ नहीं पढ़ने का फैसला किया—अज्ञानता ही सुख है।"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "Ignorance is bliss" is "You're better off not knowing" because the idiom emphasizes that avoiding certain knowledge can lead to contentment. The other options do not relate to this concept.

Conclusion:

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the idiom below.
“Boil the ocean “

(Talathi)
options: Not taking risks and keeping things simple
Scared of taking responsibilities
undertaking an impossible task
Using the ocean water effectively
solution:
The correct answer is: undertaking an impossible task

Explanation:
"Boil the ocean" - "असंभव कार्य करने का प्रयास करना"
This idiom means attempting something that is extremely difficult or outright impossible, much like trying to boil the entire ocean—an impractical and unrealistic task.

Origin of the Idiom:
The phrase likely originated as a hyperbolic expression to emphasize the futility of attempting something on an impossibly large scale. It is often used in business or project management to discourage overly ambitious or unrealistic goals.

Example:
"Trying to fix all the company's problems in one week is like trying to boil the ocean."
"एक हफ्ते में कंपनी की सारी समस्याओं को ठीक करने की कोशिश करना समुद्र को उबालने जैसा है।"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "boil the ocean" is "undertaking an impossible task" because it conveys the idea of attempting something unachievable. The other options do not align with the idiom's intended meaning.

question:
Select the option that can substitute the underlined segment with the correct idiom.
After finishing this assignment, the employees make it a day.
(Combined Graduate Level Examination Tier I 2023)
options: consider it a day
stop it a day
call it a day
ring it a day
solution:
The correct answer is: call it a day

Explanation:
The idiom "call it a day" means to decide to stop working on something for the day. In the given sentence, the employees are finishing their assignment and ending their work, which fits perfectly with this idiom.

Let's Explain All IDIOMS & Their Meanings:

"consider it a day" – "इसे एक दिन मान लो" – (Not a standard idiom; incorrect usage)
Example: "After working for hours, he decided to consider it a day." (Incorrect)

"stop it a day" – "इसे एक दिन रोक दो" – (Not an idiom; grammatically incorrect)
Example: "They wanted to stop it a day early." (Incorrect)

"call it a day" – "काम समाप्त करना" – (To stop working for the day)
Example: "After completing the project, they decided to call it a day."

"ring it a day" – "इसे एक दिन की घंटी बजाओ" – (Not a valid idiom; incorrect usage)
Example: "He wanted to ring it a day after the meeting." (Incorrect)

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "call it a day" is "to stop working for the day" because it perfectly matches the context of employees finishing their assignment and ending work. The other options are either incorrect or not valid idioms.

question:
Select the word segment that substitutes (replaces) the bracketed idiom segment correctly and completes the sentence meaningfully.

She (bit off more than she could chew) when she agreed to lead three projects.
(Statistical Assistant)
options: angered someone
took on too much work
hurt her teeth
ate too much food
solution:
The correct answer is: took on too much work

Explanation:
"bit off more than she could chew" - "जितना संभाल सकती थी, उससे ज्यादा की जिम्मेदारी ले ली"
This idiom means to take on more responsibilities or tasks than one can handle. In the given sentence, the woman agreed to lead three projects, which implies she accepted more work than she could manage.

Origin of the Idiom:
The phrase originates from the literal act of biting off more food than one can chew comfortably. Over time, it evolved into a metaphor for overcommitting or taking on excessive responsibilities.

Example:
"He regretted volunteering for two jobs at once—he had clearly bitten off more than he could chew."
"उसे दो काम एक साथ करने के लिए स्वेच्छा से सहमत होने पर पछतावा हुआ—उसने स्पष्ट रूप से अपनी क्षमता से अधिक जिम्मेदारी ले ली थी।"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "bit off more than she could chew" is "took on too much work" because it accurately describes overcommitting to tasks beyond one's capacity. The other options ("angered someone," "hurt her teeth," "ate too much food") are unrelated to the idiom's intended meaning.

question:

Still waters run deep
(Stenographer Grade C and D Examination 2023)
options: Desperate measures made in order to come out of a difficult situation
A very serious situation
To have passion or great intelligence underneath a calm expression
To be confused or not understand something
solution:
The correct answer is: To have passion or great intelligence underneath a calm expression

Explanation:
"Still waters run deep" - "शांत जल में गहराई होती है"
This idiom suggests that a person who appears calm or quiet on the surface may have deep emotions, intelligence, or complexity beneath.

Origin of the Idiom:
The phrase originates from the observation that calm, still bodies of water often conceal great depths. Similarly, a person who seems reserved may possess profound thoughts or intense feelings.

Example:
"She rarely speaks in meetings, but when she does, her ideas are brilliant—still waters run deep."
"वह मीटिंग्स में कम बोलती है, लेकिन जब बोलती है, तो उसके विचार शानदार होते हैं—शांत जल में गहराई होती है।"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "Still waters run deep" is "To have passion or great intelligence underneath a calm expression" because it refers to hidden depth beneath a quiet exterior. The other options do not relate to this idiom's meaning.

The idiom "in the limelight" refers to being the focus of public attention, much like how a performer is illuminated by a spotlight on stage. The correct option, "The centre of attraction," aligns perfectly with this meaning.

Origin of the Idiom:
The phrase originates from the 19th-century theater, where lime (calcium oxide) was burned to produce a bright light that illuminated performers on stage. Over time, it evolved to symbolize being in the public eye.

"After winning the championship, the young athlete was constantly in the limelight."
"चैंपियनशिप जीतने के बाद, युवा एथलीट लगातार ध्यान के केंद्र में रहा।"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "In the limelight" is "The centre of attention" because it signifies being widely noticed or admired. The other options do not relate to the idiom's intended meaning.

question:
Choose the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Bite the dust


(Warder Reserved for male Only)
options: To stop living
To abuse
To recall old memories
To behave weirdly
solution:
The correct answer is: To stop living

Explanation:
"Bite the dust" - "मर जाना / पराजित होना"
This idiom is commonly used to indicate death or defeat. It metaphorically suggests someone falling to the ground (biting the dust) after being killed or losing a battle.

Origin of the Idiom:
The phrase likely originates from old Western films, where cowboys or soldiers would fall to the ground after being shot, literally "biting the dust." Over time, it became a figurative expression for failure or death.

Example:
"Many soldiers bit the dust in the fierce battle."
"कड़ी लड़ाई में कई सैनिक मारे गए।"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "Bite the dust" is "To stop living" because it signifies death or defeat. The other options—abuse, recalling memories, or behaving weirdly—are unrelated to this idiom.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
It turns out to be a blessing in disguise.
(Combined Graduate Level Examination Tier I 2023)
options: Has a good effect even though at first it seemed it would be bad
When things get better and better when least expecting it
When a simple solution solves a problem very well
Has a very good effect on a situation or a thing
solution:
The correct answer is: Has a good effect even though at first it seemed it would be bad

Explanation:
"Blessing in disguise" - "छुपा हुआ वरदान"
This idiom means that something initially perceived as bad or unfortunate turns out to have a positive outcome in the end.

Origin of the Idiom:
The phrase likely originated in the 18th century, with the earliest recorded use in a poem by James Hervey. It reflects the idea that misfortunes can sometimes lead to unexpected benefits.

Example:
"Losing that job was a blessing in disguise because it pushed me to start my own business."
"वह नौकरी खोना एक छुपा हुआ वरदान था क्योंकि इसने मुझे अपना व्यवसाय शुरू करने के लिए प्रेरित किया।"

Conclusion:
The correct meaning of "It turns out to be a blessing in disguise" is "Has a good effect even though at first it seemed it would be bad" because the idiom describes a situation where an apparent setback later reveals a positive outcome. The other options do not accurately capture this meaning.
